newsitem.title: CHINA: China recalls bitter past on Japan anniversary.
newsitem.headline: China recalls bitter past on Japan anniversary.

text.p: China on Wednesday marked the 65th anniversary of the start of its invasion by Japan with strident editorials recalling the bitterness of war and demands for Tokyo to renounce past militarism.

Attempts by rightist groups to buttress Tokyo's claim to disputed islands in the East China Sea showed some Japanese were determined to reopen the seeping wounds left by a war begun in 1931 in northeastern Manchuria, the official China Daily said.

"There are still a minority of Japanese who rigidly grasp the corpse of militarism and will not let go, who return evil for good and constantly create disturbances," thundered the People's Daily, mouthpiece of Beijing's communist leadership.
China should be on its guard against any repeat of past tragedies, while some Japanese politicians continued to deny Tokyo's history of aggression, the Xinhua news agency said.
"There is still a force in Japan attempting to renew the old dream of militarism, even within its political circles," the agency quoted Foreign Minstry spokesman Shen Guofang as saying.
September 18 has long been one of the most sensitive dates in a history of Sino-Japanese relations strewn with bitter anniversaries.

The day marks the start of the occupation by Japanese troops of the region that is now known as northeastern China, and led directly to the 1937 start of an all-out invasion of the country in which tens of millions of Chinese were killed.

Anniversary tensions this year have been raised by a renewed dispute over Tokyo's control of the uninhabited but potentially resource-rich group of islands known in Chinese as the Diaoyus and in Japanese as the Senkakus.

Scores of uniformed and plainclothes police stood by at the Japanese embassy in Beijing to prevent any public expression of anger over the July construction of a lighthouse by a Japanese rightwing youth group on one of the Diaoyu islands.

Beijing, charting a delicate course between nationalist outrage and diplomatic caution, has joined rival claimant Taipei in denouncing Tokyo's failure to curb the rightwingers but has avoided accepting demands from activists for military action.

Leading anti-Japanese campaigners who planned to hold a demonstration outside the Beijing embassy have been sent on "business trips" to distant provinces that are expected to keep them far from the capital until the anniversary is safely past.
Japan's apparent official connivance with the rightist lighthouse builders was just one source of concern for Chinese still wary of Tokyo's intentions, the China Daily said.
It was clear some Japanese were still trying to damage Sino-Japanese ties, the newspaper said.
"With one hand busily trying to cover their younger generation's eyes from the historic facts, they are using another hand to pull the scab right off the sore," it said.
A cartoon alongside the commentary showed two Japanese, one armed with a rifle and blood-soaked bayonet, standing over a placard proclaiming Tokyo's ownership of the Diaoyus.
China was demanding Japan acknowledge its historical aggression and carry out a sincere self-examination of its wartime actions, the People's Daily said.

Lingering militarist sentiment had been illustrated by repeated denials by some Japanese leaders of the 1937 massacre of civilians in China's eastern city of Nanjing and by visits by senior politicians to a Tokyo shrine to Japan's war dead.
Xinhua said the United States had failed to pursue all Japanese war criminals after the war and said Japan was quickly becoming a political and military powerhouse.
Tokyo's military expenditure in 1995 was the second highest in the world and some of its forces were on a par with those of the United States, the news agency said.
"The people of Asia are watching closely the policies Japan will adopt," it said.
